Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA Iran Iran claims to have attacked 10 ships near strait of Hormuz after US strikes Oil price rises above $100 a barrel as Tehran responds to US attacks that sunk five Iranian tankers William Christou Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.32 EDT Last modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.33 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Tehran has said it attacked 10 ships around the strait of Hormuz after the US sunk five Iranian tankers, as escalating strikes between the two sent the oil price over $100 a barrel for the first time since July. The attacks were the sharpest flare-up of strikes in weeks, as the two sides struggled to break a deadlock in the six-month-long war. Fighting in recent weeks has largely revolved around who controls the strait of Hormuz, as Iran attempts to close off the waterway and Washington enforces a blockade of Iranian ports. The strait is a critical route for global energy supplies, with up to 20% of the world’s oil and gas transiting it before the US-Iran war. The rising price of oil, above the psychologically significant $100 mark is likely to have knock-on effects on inflation and the price of goods. Stocks fell on Wall Street while rising fuel and food prices in the US will further frustrate the Trump administration, which faces a midterm election with an unpopular war and a cost-of-living crisis. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday that it had attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers and 10 “noncompliant vessels” near the strait – a likely reference to ships that tried to traverse the waterway without its permission. At least one sailor was killed and another was missing. The US denied that its vessels were hit, with US Central Command saying in a post on social media that all “attempted attacks failed”. A tanker in Iraqi waters carrying 2mi barrels of fuel oil was also struck by a drone, according to Iraqi officials. There were no reports of casualties among the crew and the Iraqi government said there were no reported oil leaks. Iran said it also fired missiles at US bases in Jordan – 18 of which authorities said were intercepted while two fell in unpopulated areas. View image in fullscreen Commercial vessels remain anchored off Bandar Abbas. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images The US had said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, publishing videos of ships on fire. The US military said the attacks were a response to Iran targeting a US navy warship twice in the previous two days, the military said. Iranian state TV said the US strikes had followed a “complex intelligence and operational action at dawn” to seize a US underwater drone in the strait. The US said that the seized craft was a “defective” older model that did not carry any sensitive data. The back-and-forth strikes signaled an intensifying escalation between the two sides as Washington announced a new policy of attacking Iranian tankers if Iran targets its warships. “Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio , told reporters. Iran said that it would also escalate its attacks, and that for every two or three tankers struck it would respond by hitting 20. The IRGC also said it would also release maps of a new, much-larger area near the strait that it considers forbidden for ships to traverse, extending as far as the Gulf off Chabahar for the first time. The conflict has also taken on an increasingly regional dimension as the Iran-aligned Houthi movement in Yemen traded strikes with Saudi Arabia. The Houthis launched a wave of attacks on four cities in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, causing large fires at oil installations and wounding 73 people. The Houthis said dozens of people have been killed in Saudi airstrikes, something unconfirmed by Riyadh. Fighting re-ignited between the two sides after the Houthis launched an offensive against the Saudi-backed government of Yemen in south Yemen last week, aimed at reaching the Red Sea. The group is trying to enforce a Red Sea blockade against Saudi Arabia, announced in July. If enforced, it would cut off another route for the kingdom to export its oil. Photograph: Stephani Spindel/UPI/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Anthony Albanese said the incident was a ‘wake-up call’ about the risks of AI. Photograph: Stephani Spindel/UPI/Shutterstock Australian politics PM rejects ‘nonsense’ suggestion he delayed revealing OpenAI Medicare hack as Labor considers changing laws Expert says Australia’s criminal laws should be clarified to determine how fault is applied to a corporation when its AI agent commits a crime Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Krishani Dhanji Fri 25 Sep 2026 01.57 EDT First published on Fri 25 Sep 2026 01.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The federal government could change Australian laws if the current legal framework could not respond to the unprecedented OpenAI hack of Medicare , ministers have confirmed. It comes as the prime minister denied accusations from the opposition he had held on to the information before announcing it at the UN general assembly in New York, and said it was released at the first possible opportunity. “It’s just nonsense … I was informed while I’ve been in New York,” Anthony Albanese told News24 on Friday. “Imagine if we had said there’s been a data breach, but we don’t know what has been sourced, we don’t know if your personal information is out there, that would have created a great deal of anxiety, which was unnecessary. “We had to ascertain the facts, and then we made the statements, as a matter of urgency, we also provided briefings to the opposition, as is appropriate.” ‘We can’t ignore AI or prevent it,’ Anthony Albanese tells UN general assembly – video The government services minister, Katy Gallagher, said she was informed about the breach on 17 September. Guardian Australia understands she informed the prime minister between Friday 18 and Saturday 19 September. Albanese left for the US on the Friday, where he first met Apple’s executive chair, Tim Cook, in California on Saturday morning, before flying to New York that afternoon. On Friday, the government said the review by spy agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, would consider whether legislative change was needed after Albanese revealed an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare’s statistics website and three other systems in June. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email If current laws could not touch the tech company, they would need updating, environment minister, Murray, Watt said on Friday. “There’s now a review of this under way through that taskforce that we’ve appointed, and one of the things that they’ll be looking at is whether these matters can be referred to the Australian federal police under current Australian law,” he told Channel Seven’s Sunrise program. “If that is possible to happen, then that will happen. If it’s not possible, then clearly that indicates that we need to change Australian laws, and that’s what we’ll be doing.” The assistant minister for technology and the digital economy, Andrew Charlton, acknowledged similar incidents would become “more and more prevalent into the future” and the government would need to be prepared. “That’s why we’re conducting a review of the incident as well as a review of the laws to determine exactly … whether there needs to be legislative change to recognise this type of incident conducted by an AI agent rather than directly by a person or a company,” Charlton told ABC radio. An OpenAI agent infiltrated Medicare – and Australia only found out months later. Here’s what we know so far Read more Albanese told the Asia Society on Thursday that the incident was a “wake-up call” about the risks of AI, and whether humans would remain in charge of the technology. “This technology is moving very, very fast, and we need to make sure that we have a responsibility to keep on top of it,” Albanese said. Labor has announced it would legislate an AI standard, which Charlton said would be informed by the rapid review. The government has said it wants the bill to be introduced by the end of the year. UNSW professor Lyria Bennett Moses, an academic expert in technology and law, said Australia’s criminal laws should be clarified to determine how fault, such as intention or knowledge, is applied to a corporation when its AI agent commits a crime. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion Rogue AI hacks government system in world first – podcast Read more She said existing laws are clear if a human or corporation gains unauthorised access to restricted data, but it’s more complicated when an AI agent commits the physical element of the offence. “The person is not the AI agent, so it’s not about what the AI agent intended. It’s about how you attribute that intention and that knowledge back to a corporation,” Bennett Moses said. Bennett Moses said existing civil laws are more likely to deal with these sorts of incidents, that would allow a government or individual to seek compensation an AI company for harm “negligently caused by that corporation”. “If their systems have suffered harm and there is financial loss, and that harm was caused by the negligence of a corporation, you’ve got a potential for litigation to get compensation for that harm,” she said. “Here it seems to me much easier to hold a company liable, because if a company caused the harm, it’s not a defence to say that my bot did it.” Independent senator, David Pocock said the incident “raises serious questions” for the government after it initially, in 2024, considered mandatory guidelines for high-risk AI but then dropped them in late 2025. “It’s great to see the PM on the world stage saying that we need global cooperation on this. We absolutely do. This is a huge challenge facing us. But it’s a bit rich where at home you’ve shelved plans for an AI safety act.” The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told reporters the Coalition would be open to working with the government to hold companies accountable. “I’ve long believed that data breaches need to be dealt with in an appropriate way and those responsible for the data breaches need to be accountable for it … But we’ll wait and see what the government has in mind.” OpenAI spokesperson, Drew Pusateri, said on Thursday the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity during training and evaluation” and was “notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems”. “During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,” Pusateri said in a statement. Pusateri said OpenAI was supporting investigations and that its review was ongoing, adding it was committed “sharing what we learn as that work continues”. https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/men.text: Anger was growing on Sunday at Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank after European diplomats and an American journalist were caught up in the unrest. Visitors from France, Belgium and Poland were among those targeted by masked settlers near the village of Taybeh on Saturday. It came a day after Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine suffered serious injuries when she was attacked by Israeli settlers. The EU on Sunday demanded “effective measures” from Israel to stop the unrest. Poland said the attack in Taybeh, a Christian village, was evidence of what Palestinians in the West Bank face on a daily basis. “The attack should be met with a firm response from the Israeli authorities,” the Polish Foreign Ministry said. US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee demanded arrests and the prosecution of those responsible after the attack on the journalist. “Attacking a female photographer is a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards,” Mr Huckabee said in a post on X early on Sunday. “Dishonourable act of senseless violence.” The US envoy said Ms Levine had been clearly identified as a journalist and was unarmed. He called for those involved to spend years in prison and demanded prosecution “to the fullest extent of the law”. The Washington Post said Ms Levine was attacked when “dozens of masked settlers” set fire to shrubs and threw rocks in a “co-ordinated assault” on Palestinian olive harvesters. “She was knocked to the ground, kicked repeatedly and stripped of her cameras and phone,” the paper said. Ms Levine was later taken to hospital in Ramallah. Photos showed her lying on a trolley with a wound dressing on the left leg and a gash on her right knee, among other injuries. On Sunday, the Post welcomed the support of the US ambassador. “We appreciate the support we’ve gotten today for our photographer, Heidi Levine, after the brutal and unwarranted attack on her. We reiterate the call for action from the government. Press freedoms are a cornerstone for democracies,” editor Matt Murray wrote on X. The attack comes amid renewed international concern over Israeli settler violence in the West Bank, after European diplomats and a French mayor were assaulted by masked people in a separate incident on Saturday. Belgium criticised the attack on its consul general and the other diplomats and urged Israel to bring those responsible to justice. Poland’s Foreign Ministry said preliminary evidence indicated Israeli settlers were responsible for the assault. Polish diplomats travelling in the convoy were unharmed, the ministry said. “We expect the Israeli authorities to provide urgent and detailed explanations, identify those responsible and ensure that they are held accountable,” it added. “We also expect effective measures to be taken to prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future.” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the mayor of a French town had also been assaulted by what he described as “extremist settlers” during Saturday’s incident. He called on Israeli authorities to stop the violence. Israeli President Isaac Herzog called Ms Levine to apologise for the attack and urged an investigation. The Israeli military described the violence as intolerable and said the incidents would be investigated. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said the circumstances remained unclear and more evidence was needed before responsibility could be established. It also noted that the diplomats’ visit had not been co-ordinated with Israeli security officials. Britain, France, Canada and other countries announced sanctions focused on Israeli settlements last month, while the US said it would not join those measures.
